M01.title: Continuation and intention identity
observations: runs/continuation.json: returncode 0; revision 2; seen [endA, next]
event endA: outcome applied, rule terminal-result, before_revision 0 -> after_revision 1
after endA: state.records.A.lifecycle = ended; state.records.A.outcome = failed; state.records.B.lifecycle = running
after endA: state.responses.endA = {owner: steward, state: pending, record: A, intention: I, evidence: 'synthetic operator selected end'}
event next: outcome applied, rule choose-subsequent-work (args response=endA, role=steward, new_record=C), after_revision 2
guards satisfied for next: state.config.next_work_roles includes steward; state.roles.steward exists; state.responses.endA.owner == steward; state.responses.endA.state == pending
after next: state.records.C = {intention: I, lifecycle: running, outcome: null}; state.responses.endA.state = resolved
state.intentions.I unchanged throughout: {state: open, text: 'reduce CPU', valid: true}
state.records.A is not deleted or reopened; state.records.B untouched
M01.explanation: Intention I is the stable identity; records are attempts under it. Event endA ends record A with outcome failed and creates a pending response owned by steward. The response carries the intention id copied from records.A.intention. Event next consumes that response (state pending -> resolved) and creates record C whose intention is copied from responses.endA.intention. So continuation is a chain records.A.intention -> responses.endA.intention -> records.C.intention; C is a new record, not a resumption of A, and A's failed outcome persists. The chooser role is supplied by the event argument 'role' and checked against config.next_work_roles and the response owner; the engine does not authenticate who emitted the event. Model assessment (not observed): choose-subsequent-work has no guard on intentions.I.state or intentions.I.valid, so the rules would allow continuation under a closed or invalid intention.

M02.title: Blockage and recovery
observations: runs/recovery.json: returncode 0; revision 2; seen [blockA, recovered]
event blockA: applied, rule blocked-report; state.records.A.lifecycle running -> blocked; state.records.A.outcome stays null
after blockA: state.responses.blockA = {owner: orchestrator, state: pending, record: A, intention: I, evidence: 'synthetic worktree missing'}
event recovered: applied, rule recovery (args record=A, response=blockA); guard state.responses.blockA.owner == orchestrator
after recovered: state.records.A.lifecycle = running; state.responses.blockA.state = resolved; no new record created
state.intentions.I and state.records.B unchanged; before_hash of recovered equals after_hash of blockA
M02.explanation: Blockage is not terminal: record A keeps its identity and null outcome, its lifecycle flips to blocked, and a pending response is created owned by orchestrator (contrast: end creates a steward-owned response). Recovery resolves that response and returns the same record to running; no continuation record is created. Model assessment: the recovery rule only guards the response owner. It does not require records[record].lifecycle == blocked, responses[response].state == pending, or responses[response].record == record, so as authored it could 'recover' an unrelated record or re-resolve an already resolved response. That is a rule gap, not an observed behavior.

M03.title: Terminal failure
observations: runs/continuation.json event endA args outcome=failed: rule terminal-result; state.records.A.lifecycle = ended; state.records.A.outcome = failed; state.responses.endA.owner = steward
runs/completions.json events endA/endB args outcome=succeeded: same rule terminal-result; state.responses.endA.owner = steward and state.responses.endB.owner = steward
terminal-result guard: records[record].lifecycle not_equals ended (any non-ended lifecycle, including blocked, is accepted by the rule text)
terminal-result effects do not read or branch on the outcome argument; state.intentions.I.state remains open after a failed end
M03.explanation: Terminal failure of a record is recorded as lifecycle ended plus outcome failed, and it is handled identically to success: one terminal-result rule, one steward-owned pending response. Failure of a record does not fail or close the intention; intentions.I stays open and valid, and record B continues running. The outcome value is stored but never consulted by any rule, so the model records terminal failure without giving it distinct consequences. Model assessment: the not_equals ended guard means a blocked record could be ended directly; whether that is intended is not stated in the data.

M04.title: Checkpoint restart
observations: runs/checkpoint-save.json: returncode 0; revision 1; seen [blockA]; receipts [blockA applied, rule blocked-report]; checkpoint.json written with keys engine, model_hash, revision, state, seen, receipts, scope
runs/checkpoint-resume.json: separate process; returncode 0; revision 1; seen [blockA]; receipts [] (no events replayed)
resume state equals saved state; model_hash equal (3d9d24b5dacace81...)
recovered state: state.records.A.lifecycle = blocked; state.responses.blockA = {owner: orchestrator, state: pending, record: A, intention: I, evidence: 'synthetic no venue'}
replay.run raises checkpoint-model-mismatch if checkpoint.model_hash differs from the fixture model digest (code path, not exercised)
M04.explanation: A fresh process recovers the exact state, revision, and seen-event set: the pending orchestrator-owned response for record A survives the restart as data, and duplicate-event protection survives via 'seen'. This shows that responsibility is represented as persisted state (an owner label on a response), not as something held in a live session. It does not show that any orchestrator picks the response up after restart: resume replayed zero events, the model has no liveness rules, and the owner field is a string with no session or process identity attached. Resumption is also guarded by the model hash, so state is only portable to the same model.

M05.title: Multiple completions
observations: runs/completions.json: returncode 0; revision 3; seen [endA, endB, reviewA]; no rejected receipts
endA applied (terminal-result): state.records.A = {intention: I, lifecycle: ended, outcome: succeeded}; state.responses.endA pending, owner steward
endB applied (terminal-result): state.records.B = {intention: I, lifecycle: ended, outcome: succeeded}; state.responses.endB pending, owner steward
reviewA applied (consider-completion, args response=endA): state.responses.endA.state = resolved
pending work at end: state.responses.endB.state = pending (owner steward); state.intentions.I.state = open
consider-completion has no guards; its only effect is set responses[response].state = resolved (set requires the key to exist)
M05.explanation: Two records under the same intention both end succeeded, each producing its own steward-owned response. Only endA was considered, so responses.endB remains pending work and intention I stays open; the model has no rule that closes an intention or reconciles two completions. Ordering matters because consider-completion uses a 'set' effect: a consider event arriving before the matching end would be rejected with missing-update-target since the response key would not exist. Model assessment: consider-completion has no guards on owner or pending state, so as authored it can re-resolve an already resolved response or one owned by orchestrator.

M06.title: Two interfaces answering one decision
observations: runs/decision.json: returncode 1 (one rejected receipt); revision 1; seen [chat]
event chat (expect_revision 0): applied, rule answer-decision; guard state.decisions.D.answer == null held
after chat: state.decisions.D = {owner: orchestrator, answer: 'end failed'} (owner changed from operator to orchestrator)
event desk (expect_revision 0): rejected, reason stale-revision; before_revision 1 == after_revision 1; before_hash == after_hash (19f808e9...)
state.decisions.D.answer remains 'end failed'; the value 'keep trying' never enters state
no field in state records which interface answered; only the receipt event id 'chat' shows it
M06.explanation: Both interfaces submitted an answer against revision 0. The first (chat) applied and set the answer; the second (desk) was rejected before any rule ran because its expected revision was stale. Had it carried no expect_revision it would still have been rejected, this time by the guard answer == null with reason no-enabled-rule. Either way the first-arriving answer wins and the state is untouched by the loser, so ordering, not interface, decides the outcome. The authored rule also moves the decision owner from operator to orchestrator upon answering; the data does not say what that transfer means. Model assessment: the state does not record the answering interface, so the fact that chat answered is recoverable only from receipts.

M07.title: Routing configuration
observations: fixture diff route-on vs route-off: only model.initial.config.desk true -> false; model_hash 3d9d24b5... vs 7675467d...
runs/route-on.json: event route applied, rule route-with-dial; state.pulse = [{intention: I, desk: true}]; revision 1
runs/route-off.json: event route applied, rule route-with-dial; state.pulse = [{intention: I, desk: false}]; revision 1
in both runs: state.records, state.responses, state.decisions, state.roles unchanged; same rule id; returncode 0
route-with-dial has no guards and one append effect that copies state.config.desk into the pulse entry
M07.explanation: The dial changes only what is recorded on the pulse entry. The same rule fires, the same revision results, and nothing else in state differs. The model gives desk=false no behavioral consequence: no alternate target, no rejection, no owner change. So in this model routing configuration is a recorded flag, not a switch that alters transitions. Model assessment: route-with-dial does not check that the intention exists, so it would append a pulse for an unknown intention.

M08.title: Launch versus drive
observations: runs/roles.json: fixture has zero events; revision 0; receipts []; returncode 0
state.roles.assistant = {start: user, drive: user}; state.roles.architect = {start: user, drive: user}
state.roles.orchestrator = {start: user, drive: autonomous}; state.roles.steward = {start: event, drive: autonomous}
no rule in the model reads roles.*.start or roles.*.drive; choose-subsequent-work only checks roles[role] exists
runs/continuation.json: the steward-owned response is created by event endA and consumed by event next with role=steward, consistent with steward.start = event but not enforced by it
M08.explanation: The roles table separates who starts an agent from what drives its later actions. Assistant and architect are user-started and user-driven; orchestrator is user-started but autonomous afterwards; steward is started by an event and runs autonomously. The roles scenario is static: it replays no events and so demonstrates only the declared table. Nothing in the rules enforces start or drive; the only runtime use of roles is an existence check in choose-subsequent-work. The launch/drive distinction is therefore authored documentation inside the state, and the continuation run is merely consistent with it.

unsettled.title: Unsettled events (model coverage)
observations: runs/unsettled.json: returncode 1; revision 0; seen []
event threshold (kind threshold-reached): rejected, reason no-enabled-rule; before_hash == after_hash (fb12129e...)
event cancel (kind cancel): rejected, reason no-enabled-rule; state unchanged
model rules only handle kinds: blocked, recover, end, choose, consider, answer, route
unsettled.explanation: Both events were rejected because no rule matches their kind, so the model does not cover threshold-based stopping or cancellation. The engine behaved correctly; the rejection is a coverage result, not an engine or task failure. Design discussion is needed on whether a threshold ends a record (and with what outcome and response owner), whether cancel is distinct from end with a cancelled outcome, who may cancel (user-driven versus autonomous roles), and whether either should touch the intention. Because rejection happened at rule matching, the run says nothing about whether record A would have qualified.

E01.title: Provenance and changed extraction assumption
observations: runs/evaluate.json: outcome satisfies; checked_events [choose]; out_of_scope_events [end]; computed_revision 0; saved_as evidence-check; saved_revision 1; result_state current; checker_version exclusive-actor/3
evaluate provenance.nodes [c, extract, source, t]; provenance.edges trace-edge, source-edge; input_fingerprints for c, t, extract, source, steward-role, orchestrator-role, choose-work, end-attempt
runs/inspect-before.json: graph revision 1; results[0].id evidence-check; result_state current

runs/apply-assumption.json: {changes: 4, revision: 2}; revision-2 edits: nodes.extract.provenance.assumptions[0] 'Ordering reflects the described sequence.' -> 'Ordering is not established by the original source.'; nodes.extract.semantic_version = 2; nodes.extract.meta.review_state = needs-review; nodes.t.meta.review_state = needs-review (reason: declared semantic prerequisite changed: extract)

runs/inspect-after.json: graph revision 2; result_state stale; outcome still satisfies; computed_revision still 0; input_fingerprints.extract still c7d13c54... while current fingerprint of extract is 587ec076...

after apply: nodes.t.trace.events unchanged (choose still has after: end); nodes.c.status still proposed; nodes.evidence-check.meta.review_state still 'current' even though derived result_state is stale
E01.explanation: The check's inputs are claim c (exclusive_actor pattern: only steward-role may choose-work after an attempt ended), trace t (events end by o1/orchestrator-role, then choose by s1/steward-role with after: end), and the declared provenance chain t -> extract -> source. The result 'satisfies' means the one checked event has the allowed role; the end event is out of scope. Applying the assumption edit changed only the extraction's provenance text, but the checker fingerprints extract as an input, so the saved result is now reported stale by tracecheck. The software also flagged extract and its dependent t as needs-review. It does not re-run the evaluation, change the outcome, revise the trace's 'after: end' ordering that the new assumption undermines, alter the claim status, or update the saved node's own meta.review_state. Deciding whether trace t still stands and re-evaluating is a human step.

E07.title: Synthetic versus historical evidence
observations: runs/node-source.json: nodes.source.meta.synthetic = true; nodes.source.meta.source_kind = synthetic-fixture; text: 'Synthetic illustration: operator ended attempt; steward chose next. No actual historical incident is supplied.'
runs/node-extract.json: nodes.extract.text = 'Interpretation of the synthetic sequence, not the source itself.'; status proposed; author fixture-author

runs/evaluate.json: synthetic true; assessment.empirical_support false; assessment.historical_behavior not-established; assessment.evidence_basis recorded-events; claim_standing proposed; pattern_standing proposed
revision-1 change reason: 'Save finite-trace pattern evaluation; do not change belief status'
E07.explanation: The source is a synthetic fixture, not historical evidence. It says so in its own metadata and text, and the checker propagated that: the result is marked synthetic, empirical support is false, and historical behavior is not-established. The 'satisfies' outcome therefore shows only that an authored trace is consistent with an authored pattern, a self-consistency check, and it changed no belief status; claim c remains proposed.

unresolved_policy: What threshold-reached and cancel should do (terminal or not, which outcome, which response owner, who may issue them).
Whether recovery must require lifecycle blocked, a pending response, and a response that references the same record.
Whether consider-completion must require steward ownership and pending state.
How multiple completions of one intention are reconciled and when, if ever, an intention closes or is invalidated.
What the transfer of decision owner from operator to orchestrator on answer means, and whether the answering interface should be recorded in state.
What desk=false is supposed to change behaviorally; the model records the dial without consequences.
Whether roles.*.start and roles.*.drive should constrain any transition, since no rule reads them.
Whether a response owner denotes a role or a session, and how a restarted process is expected to pick up pending responses.
Whether trace t's ordering (choose after end) remains justified now that the extraction says ordering is not established by the original source, and who re-evaluates.
limitations: All results are replays of explicitly authored finite transitions on the supplied fixtures; they prove nothing about all executions, liveness, or a Morphisms runtime.
Event arguments assert roles; the engine does not authenticate actors, so 'steward chose' means only that the event said role=steward and the guards accepted it.
The checkpoint resume replayed zero events, so persistence was shown but post-restart handling was not.
The evidence graph is a synthetic fixture; the exclusive-actor checker checks one pattern kind on one trace and does not assess trace truth.
The stale/current freshness is derived at read time by tracecheck; the saved node's meta.review_state is not kept in sync by the software.
The eight scenarios share one model except route-off (config.desk only); observations about rule gaps are assessments of the authored rules, not observed misbehavior.
Receipts under runs/ capture stdout, stderr, exit code and elapsed time only; elapsed times are not meaningful measurements.
